actions.action: Choose plants hardy for your USDA zone
Assess property for cold and warm spots and microclimates
Place cold-sensitive plants near southern exposure or sheltering structures
Apply a winterizing high-potassium, low-nitrogen fertilizer
Set up windbreaks such as fences or temporary coverings
Move container plants into a protective structure
Push outdoor containers together and wrap their bases in plastic, burlap or blankets
Cover plants with sheets or blankets reaching the ground without touching foliage
Place a 60-watt bulb or other heat source under the cover in extreme cold
Remove covers and ventilate during the day or after the cold passes
Check water needs after a freeze and water to thaw frozen soil
Wait until late winter or early spring, then prune damaged portions
Scratch the bark to check the cambium and prune below the discoloration
Cut fruit buds in cross section to check for cold damage

verdict.reason: This is a generic outdoor cold-injury article rather than a diagnosis of this plant, so it only partially matches the cold damage. It omits the fix (cutting back near the soil, withholding water, using a humidity jar), and its advice to water after a freeze and delay pruning until spring would likely worsen or delay recovery.
